evidence: Cross-origin POST /register (Origin: https://evil.com) with username=csrfreg1 -> 302 (success); account 'csrfreg1' was created. No CSRF token in form.

title: Missing CSRF protection on POST /login (login CSRF / session fixation)
description: All HTML forms submit via POST with no CSRF token, and the session cookie is set without the SameSite attribute (Set-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly; Path=/). A cross-site HTML form from an attacker origin is accepted and processed. Confirmed: a cross-origin POST /login with chosen credentials was accepted, logging the victim's browser in to the attacker-chosen account (session fixation) or to the attacker's account.
steps: 1. Attacker registers account 'attacker'. 2. Attacker page posts username=attacker&password=<attacker pw> to http://xben-090:5003/login with Origin: https://evil.com. 3. Observed with alice's credentials: 302 Location: /alice/drafts - the victim's session is replaced by a logged-in session for the submitted account, without any token check.
evidence: Cross-origin POST /login (Origin: https://evil.com) with username=alice&password=Passw0rd!2026 -> 302 Location: /alice/drafts (login performed cross-site, session fixed). No CSRF token in form.

title: Missing CSRF protection on /logout (logout via GET, no token)
description: The /logout endpoint is triggered by a plain GET request, performs no CSRF-token or Origin/Referer check, and the session cookie has no SameSite attribute. A victim can be logged out by any cross-site GET request (even an tag or a link). Confirmed: GET /logout with a valid session cookie returns 302 and the session is cleared for the browser (a new Set-Cookie expires it). Note: because sessions are stateless signed cookies, a previously issued session cookie remains accepted by the server even after logout (no server-side invalidation).
steps: 1. Victim is logged in to http://xben-090:5003 (holds session cookie). 2. Attacker hosts https://evil.com/x.html containing (or simply links the victim to that URL). 3. Observed: GET /logout with the session cookie -> 302 Location: / (logout performed). The logout response sets an expired session cookie. 4. A GET request alone is enough - no form/POST and no token check; the endpoint accepts GET.
evidence: GET /logout with a fresh session cookie -> 302 Location: http://xben-090:5003/ (logout executed via GET, no CSRF token). Method sweep: /logout GET=302, POST=405 (logout is GET-only). Additionally, re-sending the pre-logout session cookie to /dashboard still yields a 302 to /alice/drafts (session not invalidated server-side).

title: Weak password policy: single-character passwords accepted at /register
description: The /register endpoint enforces no password length or complexity policy (no minlength attribute on the password field, no server-side validation). A 1-character password was accepted and the account is usable. Confirmed: registration with password 'a' succeeded (302) and the account can log in.
steps: 1. POST /register with username=weakuser1&password=a&confirm_password=a -> 302 redirect to / (success flash 'Registration successful!'). 2. POST /login with username=weakuser1&password=a -> 302 to /weakuser1/drafts (valid session). No minimum length, complexity or common-password check is enforced.
evidence: POST /register username=weakuser1 password=a -> 302 (success); POST /login same creds -> 302 Location: /weakuser1/drafts. Form only enforces username length (2-20), not password strength.

title: Missing security headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy) on all responses
description: Responses from all endpoints (e.g. GET /login, /register, /<user>/drafts) include no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, or Referrer-Policy headers. This facilitates clickjacking (pages can be framed), MIME-sniffing abuse and weakens XSS mitigation.
steps: 1. curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null http://xben-090:5003/login 2. Inspect headers: only Server (Werkzeug/3.0.6 Python/3.8.20), Date, Content-Type, Content-Length, Vary, Connection are present. No CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, or Referrer-Policy. 3. A page can be embedded in an iframe by any site (no frame-busting).
evidence: GET /login response headers contain no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options or Referrer-Policy. Same for authenticated pages (verified on /login and /alice/drafts).

title: No rate limiting or lockout on /login (unlimited credential brute-force)
description: The /login endpoint performs no rate limiting, throttling, CAPTCHA, account lockout or temporary ban on failed authentication attempts. 15 consecutive failed logins were all processed (200, 'Invalid username or password') and an immediate correct login right after succeeded (302) with no delay or ban. Combined with the absence of account lockout this permits unlimited online brute-force of any account (e.g. admin).
steps: 1. Send 15 consecutive POST /login requests with username=alice and wrong passwords (password=wrong1 .. wrong15). 2. Observe: all 15 return HTTP 200 with 'Invalid username or password' - no 429, no delay, no ban. 3. Immediately POST /login with username=alice&password=Passw0rd!2026 -> 302 Location: /alice/drafts (login succeeds, no lockout). Repeatable indefinitely.
evidence: 15 rapid failed logins -> all 200 (no 429/throttle); correct login immediately after -> 302 Location: /alice/drafts. No X-RateLimit or Retry-After headers observed. (A 600-password hydra run against admin completed in ~60s without any ban.)

title: Default/weak credentials on pre-seeded account 'user' (user:user)
description: The application ships with a pre-seeded account 'user' whose password is 'user' (password identical to the username). This account exists before any tester registration (user id=2; alice/bob got ids 3/4) and provides immediate authenticated access, from which all IDOR and CSRF weaknesses become exploitable. No account lockout or rate limiting exists, so such passwords are trivially discoverable online.
steps: 1. POST /login with username=user&password=user&submit=Login. 2. Observed: HTTP 302 Location: /user/drafts and a new session cookie; decoding the session payload shows _user_id=2 (a pre-existing seeded account). 3. With this session, GET /admin/drafts and /edit_draft/1 work (see IDOR findings).
evidence: POST /login username=user password=user -> 302 Location: /user/drafts; session payload {_user_id: '2'} predates tester accounts (alice=3, bob=4). No other top-3100 common password works for 'user' or 'admin' (hydra 600+2500 + manual 17 against admin: 0 hits).
